What Is BMI and How Is It Calculated? A Simple Guide

27 October 2025 · 3 min read · Health

Body Mass Index (BMI) is the most widely used first-pass screen for whether a person's weight is in a healthy range for their height. Doctors, insurers and fitness apps all quote it — yet most people have never seen the actual calculation. It takes ten seconds.

The formula

BMI is weight in kilograms divided by height in metres, squared:

BMI = weight (kg) ÷ height² (m²)

That's the entire formula. No age, no gender, no body-fat measurement — just two numbers.

A worked example

Take someone who weighs 70 kg and is 1.75 m tall:

  1. Square the height: 1.75 × 1.75 = 3.0625
  2. Divide the weight by that: 70 ÷ 3.0625 = 22.9

A BMI of 22.9 lands squarely in the "normal weight" band.

If your measurements are in other units, convert first: 1 kg ≈ 2.2046 lb and 1 m ≈ 3.2808 ft. The BMI Calculator accepts metric inputs and shows your category instantly.

The WHO categories

The World Health Organization's adult classification is:

  • Underweight — below 18.5
  • Normal weight — 18.5 to 24.9
  • Overweight — 25.0 to 29.9
  • Obesity — 30.0 and above

These bands are population-level screening thresholds, not diagnostic verdicts. A BMI of 26 is a prompt to look closer — at waist measurement, activity, blood work — not a label.

South Asian cut-offs

Several health bodies use lower thresholds for South Asian populations because cardiometabolic risk rises at lower BMI: overweight from 23 and obesity from 25. If you are from Nepal, India or the region, mention this to your doctor — a "normal" WHO number can still warrant attention.

What BMI gets right

  • It is consistent. Two numbers, one formula, no equipment — so trends over months and years are comparable.
  • It correlates. At a population level, higher BMI tracks with higher rates of type-2 diabetes, hypertension and cardiovascular disease.
  • It is free. No lab, no scan, no subscription — which is exactly why it became the global default screen.

What BMI gets wrong

  • It cannot see muscle. A muscular 80 kg athlete at 1.75 m reads as "overweight" (BMI 26.1) despite low body fat. Weightlifters routinely "fail" the test.
  • It ignores fat distribution. Visceral fat around the waist carries more risk than the same weight carried elsewhere; waist circumference adds information BMI cannot.
  • It is not for everyone. The adult bands do not apply to children (who use age-and-sex growth charts), pregnant women, or the very elderly, where weight loss can be the bigger risk.

A healthy way to use it

Treat BMI the way a smoke alarm works: cheap, always on, and good at saying look closer — not at telling you what's burning. A sensible routine is:

  1. Check BMI once every few months, not daily.
  2. Track the trend, and pair it with waist measurement.
  3. If the number drifts out of range — or sits "normal" while your waist grows — talk to a professional about the full picture: diet, activity, sleep and blood markers.

The takeaway

BMI is two divisions away from a useful, free screening signal — and exactly one step removed from a diagnosis. Calculate it, log the trend, and let a professional interpret the rest.
